proposal: The Mandate says CISA's funding should align narrowly with protecting federal civilian networks and coordinating critical infrastructure security, that its counter-misinformation and disinformation work should end immediately and its Cybersecurity Advisory Committee be dismissed on day one, and that its election role be limited to hygiene assessments. It would move emergency communications and chemical facility standards to FEMA, school security to states, and CISA itself to the Department of Transportation.

status_summary: Parts of the narrowing are operative and parts are only proposed: CISA lost about a third of its workforce after January 2025 (Cybersecurity Dive, 2026-02-12), election-security and foreign-influence/disinformation staff were reported placed on administrative leave in a state official's letter of 2025-02-12, and DHS ended all advisory committee memberships on 2025-01-20 (sources reviewed name the Cyber Safety Review Board but not the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee). The FY2027 budget request of 2026-04-07, which Congress has not enacted, would per Cybersecurity Dive cut a net 386 million dollars and 867 positions, end the chemical facilities inspection program and the 14-position election security program and close the Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Nextgov adds the end of dedicated election security advisors and support for the election information-sharing center; SecurityWeek reports a 707 million dollar cut that also terminates programs focused on combating misinformation, a point the other two reports of that date do not describe, and a CRS analysis of 2026-06-09 states the request as 2.49 billion dollars, 386 million below the FY2025 continuing-resolution level. No proposal to move CISA to Transportation, or emergency communications and chemical facility roles to FEMA, was found, and in June 2026 DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin described plans for structural change while seeking to hire up to 600 more staff. On 2026-09-24 CISA released a 2026 election infrastructure security plan that relies on regional directors and threat-sharing tools and does not restore dedicated election adviser positions, per Nextgov.

timeline.event: Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman issues a memo ending all memberships on DHS advisory committees, effective immediately; reports name the Cyber Safety Review Board and do not name the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee.

A letter from Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs to the state's congressional delegation reports that CISA employees in its Election Security and Resilience Division and its Foreign Influence Operations and Disinformation initiative were placed on administrative leave, and describes uncertainty over federal funding for the election-focused information sharing center (EI-ISAC).

Cybersecurity Dive reports CISA has lost about a third of its workforce since January 2025 and is preparing a Cybersecurity Division reorganization that will turn off some programs and prioritize operational technology security, cyber intelligence and collaborative defense.
DHS funding lapse begins; congressional testimony cited by CRS says CISA furloughed roughly 60 percent of staff. P.L. 119-86, enacted 2026-04-30, ended the lapse for most of DHS including CISA.

The FY2027 budget request proposes cutting about $707 million from CISA (to roughly $2 billion), dissolving the stakeholder-engagement and international affairs offices, terminating programs focused on countering misinformation and propaganda, and removing school safety initiatives; a separate outlet reports it would also eliminate the election security program and shift some infrastructure security and emergency communications responsibilities to state and local governments. SecurityWeek reports Congress had cut the proposed FY2026 reduction from $491 million to about $135 million.

Cybersecurity Dive reports that the FY2027 CISA budget justification would cut a net 386 million dollars and 867 positions (leaving 2,865), eliminate the chemical facilities inspection program (223 positions) and the 14-position election security program, close the Stakeholder Engagement Division apart from one team, and cut 63 bombing-prevention and school-safety positions; the request is not enacted.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin tells the House Homeland Security Committee CISA will undergo significant structural changes, that a Senate-confirmed director will be nominated (Nick Andersen is acting director), and that the FY2027 budget proposes cutting more than $700 million; the report does not mention relocating CISA or moving its functions to other agencies.

A CRS analysis of the FY2027 DHS request states that CISA's request is 2.49 billion dollars, 109 million above the FY2026 request and 386 million (13.4 percent) below the FY2025 continuing-resolution level, with a research and development account of 44 million dollars partly from moving Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction work to CISA; the text read does not cover election security, counter-misinformation or program eliminations, and says CISA's staffing fell sharply in the six months to March 2026.

OMB Director Russell Vought tells lawmakers he will work with Secretary Mullin on rehiring for CISA, which Mullin has said he wants to expand by 600 staff; acting director Andersen says CISA expects nearly 200 job offers by the end of June.

DHS publishes a Federal Register notice (91 FR 40022) establishing ANCHOR-CI, an advisory body of sector and cross-sector councils that advises the Secretary through the CISA Director; the notice does not mention the Cybersecurity Advisory Committee.

CISA releases its 2026 Election Infrastructure Security Plan (regional directors as election security advisers, threat-sharing platform); Nextgov notes it does not restore dedicated election adviser positions and that the FY2027 request would eliminate the election security program.

title: Narrow CISA to two core missions and end its counter-disinformation work
uncertainties: Not verified: whether the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee specifically was terminated (reports of the 2025-01-20 DHS memo name only the Cyber Safety Review Board; a Federal Register search for the committee returned no termination or meeting notice); and the date and form of the end of CISA's mis/disinformation work (evidence is staff leave reported in a state official's letter, plus SecurityWeek's report that the FY2027 request terminates such programs). The 2026 staffing figures differ across outlets (about 1,000 positions lost; a target of 2,800 staff reported against about 2,200 currently, which the source itself left unclear). An AOL copy of a report on 12 CISA employees placed on leave returned an error and was not used. Searches run: CSAC termination, CISA election and disinformation staff, CISA director and FY2027 budget; no search found any proposal to move CISA to Transportation. The DHS FY2027 CISA budget document and the DHS Budget in Brief (dhs.gov; dates taken from file names) were not opened: in the latest check the dhs.gov CISA document returned a client error again and an archived copy on web.archive.org was blocked, so the program eliminations rest on trade reporting. Cybersecurity Dive and Nextgov (both dated 2026-04-07 and read in the latest check) agree on 867 positions and on the elimination of the election security program; Cybersecurity Dive gives a net cut of 386 million dollars and Nextgov about 360 million dollars after transfers, so the net figure differs slightly between them. An external retrieval reported a fuller account of the justification (a request of 2,487 million dollars against a FY2026 annualized continuing-resolution baseline of 2,873 million, 2,528 FTE, and no use of the words misinformation or disinformation in its 279 pages); these details are known only through that retrieval and are not stated as verified. Two conflicts remain unresolved: the baseline label (the retrieval names the FY2026 annualized continuing resolution, whereas CRS R48979 describes the 386 million dollar gap as against the FY2025 continuing-resolution level); and SecurityWeek's report that the request terminates programs combating misinformation, which the two other trade reports do not mention and the retrieval contradicts. CRS R48979 (read through its first 100,000 characters) does not reconcile with the press reports of a 707 million dollar cut to about 2 billion dollars; the comparison base for the 707 million figure was not established, so the size of the proposed cut is uncertain. Latest check (2026-10-22): the dhs.gov CISA justification and its archived copy on web.archive.org failed again in a second round (client error at dhs.gov; web.archive.org blocked by the fetch tool), so nothing from the external retrieval is verified. The retrieval also reports, unverified, that the document prints no release date (April 2026 comes from the file name and PDF metadata, with 2026-04-03 as the date in the file name), whereas the record and trade reports date the request 2026-04-07; that the net change is a decrease of 385,814 thousand dollars against the annualized continuing-resolution base; that the election security elimination is 39,610 thousand dollars and 14 positions at page CISA-O&S-30; and that a separate chemical facilities program elimination is 35,076 thousand dollars and 223 positions.
